games.title: Dungeons & Dragons
games.note: Grew out of Chainmail miniatures wargaming; its classes, hit points and experience levels became the basis of computer RPGs.

games.title: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord
games.note: Ported to Japanese computers, it became popular there and shaped Dragon Quest, Final Fantasy and Megami Tensei.

games.title: Rogue
games.dev: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman & Ken Arnold
games.note: Spread through university Unix systems; its random dungeons and permanent death gave the roguelike genre its name.

games.title: Moria
games.note: Written at the University of Oklahoma after Koeneke got hooked on Rogue; it is set in Tolkien's Mines of Moria.

games.title: Angband
games.note: Created at the University of Warwick by expanding Umoria; David Brevik called it 'the model of what we wanted' for Diablo.

games.title: NetHack
games.note: Grew out of Hack (1982) and was developed by volunteers coordinating over Usenet.

games.title: Ultima III: Exodus
games.note: The first game published by Richard Garriott's own company, Origin Systems.

games.title: The Tower of Druaga
games.note: Masanobu Endo pitched it as a 'fantasy Pac-Man'; finding each floor's hidden treasure pushed players to share tips.

games.title: Hydlide
games.note: The first action RPG with an overworld, and an early game where health regenerates while you stand still.

games.title: Dragon Slayer
games.note: Often called the first Japanese action RPG; its series later spawned Xanadu and The Legend of Heroes.

games.title: The Portopia Serial Murder Case
games.note: Yuji Horii's detective adventure; its menu of commands was reused for Dragon Quest.

games.title: Ys I: Ancient Ys Vanished
games.note: You attack by running into enemies; the soundtrack by Yuzo Koshiro and Mieko Ishikawa is still widely praised.

games.title: Minecraft
games.note: The best-selling video game of all time.

games.title: Dragon Quest II
games.note: Added a party of three heroes and a ship for sailing the world.

games.title: Dragon Quest V: Hand of the Heavenly Bride
games.note: Follows one hero across about thirty years, from childhood to fatherhood.

games.title: Dragon Quest Monsters: Terry's Wonderland
games.note: Stars a young Terry from Dragon Quest VI, who recruits and breeds monsters to win a tournament.

games.title: Dragon Quest VIII: Journey of the Cursed King
games.note: The series' first fully 3D world, cel-shaded to match Akira Toriyama's art.

games.title: Dragon Quest XI: Echoes of an Elusive Age
games.note: Its story ties back into Dragon Quest III, closing the Erdrick trilogy decades later.

games.title: Dragon Quest Builders
games.note: Set in a parallel ending of the first Dragon Quest, where the hero accepted the Dragonlord's offer.

games.title: The Final Fantasy Legend
games.note: Released in Japan as Makai Toushi SaGa, it was Square's first Game Boy game and began the SaGa series.

games.title: Mother
games.note: Written by copywriter Shigesato Itoi; released in English in 2015 as EarthBound Beginnings.

games.title: EarthBound
games.note: Released in Japan as Mother 2; its US ads used the slogan 'This game stinks.'

games.title: Mother 3
games.note: Never released outside Japan; a 2008 fan translation brought it to English-speaking players.

games.title: Undertale
games.note: Made almost entirely by Toby Fox; every monster can be spared, and the game remembers how you treated them.

games.title: Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei
games.note: Based on Aya Nishitani's novels; players talk demons into joining their party.

games.title: Shin Megami Tensei
games.note: Set in a Tokyo destroyed by missiles; choices align the hero with Law, Chaos or Neutral.

games.title: Shin Megami Tensei If...
games.note: Its high school setting proved popular enough to spin off the Persona series.

games.title: Persona 2: Innocent Sin
games.note: Rumors spread around town come true and reshape the story.

games.title: Persona 3
games.note: Added the school calendar and Social Links that define the modern Persona games.

games.title: Shin Megami Tensei III: Nocturne
games.note: Introduced the Press Turn system, where hitting a weakness earns extra actions.

games.title: Catherine
games.note: A block-climbing puzzle game about relationships, made by the Persona team between Persona 4 and 5.

games.title: Metaphor: ReFantazio
games.note: Katsura Hashino built its story around the idea of 'utopia'; its monsters draw on Hieronymus Bosch.

links.took: Party-based dungeon adventuring with classes, levels, hit points and spells.
links.added: A solo computer game of mapping a ten-level maze in first person.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord

links.extra: Wikipedia also names PLATO games such as Oubliette (1977) as influences.

links.took: Commanding a party of adventurers in combat instead of a lone hero.
links.added: Tactical grid battles and a large overworld of towns, dungeons and sailing ships.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ultima III: Exodus (Richard Garriott credits Wizardry for party combat)

links.took: Garriott's top-down overworld of towns, dungeons and a final villain to defeat.
links.added: A four-character party, separate tactical combat screens and a new publisher, Origin.

links.took: Random dungeon levels, turn-based text-character combat and permanent death.
links.added: A Tolkien-inspired setting, a surface town with shops, and a Balrog at the bottom.

src.t: Wikipedia: Moria (Koeneke 'became hooked on playing Rogue')

links.took: Umoria's code, Tolkien setting and town-above-dungeon structure.
links.added: Many more items, monsters and features, with Morgoth waiting far below.
links.extra: Warwick students Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand built it by expanding Umoria.

links.took: Character classes, spells and monster-filled dungeons from tabletop fantasy.
links.added: Real-time mouse-click combat in a gothic town above randomized catacombs.

src.t: Wikipedia: Diablo (David Brevik's idea: 'a combination of Dungeons & Dragons and the roguelike genre')

links.extra: This was Brevik's original pitch, before Blizzard asked for real-time play.

links.took: Randomly generated dungeon levels and the tension of risky descents.
links.added: Real-time action, isometric graphics and online co-op through Battle.net.

src.t: Wikipedia: Diablo (Bill Roper on the pitch: 'games like Moria, Nethack, and Rogue')

links.took: A town on the surface above a deep, randomly built dungeon.
links.added: Graphics, real-time fights and a story about the Lord of Terror beneath Tristram.

src.t: Wikipedia: Moria ('influenced the preliminary design of Blizzard Entertainment's Diablo')

links.took: Randomized levels and items, which Brevik called a huge influence.
links.added: Fast, mouse-driven real-time play that anyone could pick up.

src.t: Wikipedia: Angband (David Brevik: 'the model of what we wanted')

links.took: Randomness and the excitement of unpredictable dungeon runs.
links.added: Gothic art, sound and real-time combat instead of turn-based text graphics.

src.t: Wikipedia: Diablo (Bill Roper on the pitch)

links.took: Fantasy monsters, treasure and magic items from tabletop role-playing.
links.added: A 60-floor arcade maze where each floor hides a treasure to uncover.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Tower of Druaga (Masanobu Endo's inspirations)

links.took: Maze-crawling fantasy from a game designer Masanobu Endo was a fan of.
links.added: Real-time arcade action and a secret item puzzle on every floor.

links.took: Maze-running arcade play; Endo conceived Druaga as a 'fantasy Pac-Man'.
links.added: Sword fights, a knight who gains equipment, and hidden treasures needed to finish.

links.took: Arcade action with RPG-like treasures; Tokihiro Naito named it his main inspiration.
links.added: An open overworld, experience levels and health that regenerates when standing still.
links.extra: Both came out in 1984; Druaga reached arcades in June, Hydlide in December.

links.took: Character growth from an early Japanese computer RPG, plus its health meter.
links.added: Real-time action combat across a scrolling field.

src.t: Wikipedia: Hydlide (Naito 'inspired by' The Tower of Druaga and The Black Onyx)

links.took: The arcade hit's mix of real-time action and RPG items.
links.added: An overhead action RPG for home computers that Falcom built into a long series.
links.extra: Druaga reached arcades in June 1984; Dragon Slayer followed in September.

links.took: Real-time sword action mixed with RPG items and hidden secrets.
links.added: An open overworld, dungeons and puzzle-solving with items.

src.t: Wikipedia: The Tower of Druaga ('influential to... The Legend of Zelda')

links.extra: A historians' claim; Miyamoto's own stated influences are different.

links.took: Health that slowly recharges while the hero stands still.
links.added: Bump-into-enemies combat, a brisk pace and a strong soundtrack.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ys I: Ancient Ys Vanished

links.took: Falcom's own overhead action-RPG formula from its first hit.
links.added: A story-driven quest with quick bump-attack combat.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Slayer ('laid the foundations for the action RPG genre, including franchises such as Ys')

links.took: Arcade dungeon action with hidden items, which shaped Japan's early action RPGs.
links.added: A full story across towns, dungeons and a tower, with Falcom's music.

links.took: Overworld travel between towns and dungeons, the template Exodus laid out.
links.added: Simple menus, Akira Toriyama's art and a story built for console newcomers.

links.took: First-person, menu-driven monster battles; Yuji Horii wanted to bring Wizardry's genre to Japan.
links.added: A single hero, Toriyama's art, Koichi Sugiyama's music and a gentle difficulty curve.
links.extra: Horii and Koichi Nakamura discovered Wizardry at a Macworld expo.

links.took: Overworld exploration between towns and dungeons, part of the gameplay Horii credited to Ultima.
links.added: Japanese-language menus and storytelling designed for Famicom players.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Quest ('Horii also cited Ultima as an inspiration')

links.extra: Horii cited Ultima in general, not one specific entry.

links.took: Horii's menu-based command system, carried over from his own adventure game.
links.added: The command menu became the core of a fantasy role-playing quest.

links.took: Akitoshi Kawazu based the battle system heavily on Dungeons & Dragons.
links.added: Side-view party battles, four Light Warriors and classes chosen at the start.

links.took: Party classes and stat-driven combat from a Western RPG Kawazu loved.
links.added: A world map, an airship and a crystal-centred story from Koichi Ishii.

links.took: Sakaguchi's pitch was an RPG inspired by Ultima and Wizardry.
links.added: A long journey unlocked by ships, a canoe and finally an airship.
links.extra: The source says Ultima in general.

links.took: The console RPG template of overworld, towns, menus and turn-based battles.
links.added: A four-member party, side-view battles and selectable character classes.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Quest ('laid the fundamentals on which Final Fantasy was based')

links.extra: Dragon Quest's hit status also helped Square approve Sakaguchi's RPG.

links.took: Party-based adventuring across an overworld, credited to Exodus.
links.added: Side-view battles and Square's own crystal-and-Light-Warriors story.

links.took: First-person dungeon crawling and party mechanics based on the Wizardry series.
links.added: Modern-day demons that you can talk into joining your party.

src.t: Wikipedia: Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei

links.took: The overworld, menus, Slimes and the Erdrick bloodline.
links.added: A party of three descendants, a ship and a much larger world.

links.took: Party adventuring in the Erdrick saga.
links.added: Building your own party at a tavern, class changes and a day-night cycle.

links.took: Satoshi Tajiri's frustration while playing it inspired the idea of trading.
links.added: Trading creatures over the Game Boy link cable to complete a collection.

src.t: Wikipedia: Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow

links.took: Turn-based party battles and Toriyama's monster designs.
links.added: A story spanning three generations and monsters that offer to join you.

links.took: Recruiting defeated monsters into your party, an idea Dragon Quest V popularized.
links.added: Catching, trading and battling 151 creatures as the whole point.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Quest V (concept 'appeared in many later franchises such as Pokémon')

links.extra: No developer statement; the same article notes Megami Tensei used the idea first.

links.took: Recruiting enemy monsters into the party, which Megami Tensei did first.
links.added: Monsters that ask to join after battle and travel in the family wagon.

links.took: Monster recruiting, used here as the main way to build a party.
links.added: Breeding two monsters to create a new one, on a handheld.

links.took: Collecting and raising monsters on the Game Boy.
links.added: Dragon Quest's monster roster and breeding to combine monsters.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Quest Monsters ('often compared to the Pokémon series')

links.took: Classic turn-based Dragon Quest battles, a horse-drawn wagon and Toriyama designs.
links.added: A seamless, cel-shaded 3D world built by Level-5.

links.took: Big 3D fields and Toriyama characters rendered in full 3D.
links.added: An Unreal Engine 4 world whose story ties back into Dragon Quest III.

links.took: Alefgard, the Dragonlord, and the first game's map and monsters.
links.added: A parallel ending where the ruined world is rebuilt block by block.

links.took: Gathering materials and building with blocks in a voxel world.
links.added: Quests, story chapters, towns to grow and Dragon Quest monsters to fight.

src.t: Wikipedia: Dragon Quest Builders (IGN: mixes RPG traditions 'with Minecraft')

links.took: Block building mixed with Dragon Quest quests and towns.
links.added: Online co-op building, a free-form home island and help from Omega Force.

links.took: Dragon Quest's battle system and structure, which a colleague introduced to Itoi.
links.added: A modern American-style suburb, baseball bats and psychic powers instead of swords.

src.t: Wikipedia: Mother ('Modeled after the gameplay of the Dragon Quest series')

links.took: The modern setting, psychic powers and Itoi's offbeat humor.
links.added: A bigger, stranger world with rolling HP meters and visible enemies.

links.took: Itoi's mix of comedy and sadness and the series' battle style.
links.added: Combo hits timed to the music and a chapter-based family tragedy.

links.took: EarthBound's unsettling atmosphere, humor and SNES-era music style.
links.added: Mercy-based battles, bullet-hell dodging and a game that remembers your choices.
links.extra: Fox cites the Mother series as a whole.

links.took: Talking to enemies in battle instead of only fighting them.
links.added: Every monster can be spared through conversation, with no grinding needed.

src.t: Wikipedia: Undertale ('dialogue system was inspired by Shin Megami Tensei')

links.took: Proof that a full RPG could work on the Game Boy; Tajiri cited it.
links.added: Catching, trading and battling creatures across two linked versions.

src.t: Wikipedia: Pokémon Red, Blue, and Yellow ('influenced by Square's Game Boy game The Final Fantasy Legend')

links.took: Akitoshi Kawazu, Final Fantasy's battle designer, and Square's RPG know-how.
links.added: Mutating monsters, robots and a tower to climb, all on a handheld.
links.extra: Sold in the West under the Final Fantasy name, though it began the separate SaGa series.

links.took: Recruiting monsters into your party, which Game Informer says Megami Tensei pioneered.
links.added: Catching and collecting creatures as the goal, with trading between friends.

src.t: Wikipedia: Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei (Kimberley Wallace, Game Informer)

links.took: Demon negotiation and recruitment in a modern setting.
links.added: A ruined Tokyo and an alignment system of Law, Chaos and Neutral.
links.extra: Atlus treated it as a remake of Megami Tensei II.

links.took: Demon negotiation, demon fusion and dungeon crawling.
links.added: A high school swallowed into a demon world.

links.took: A high school setting, popular enough to start a new subseries.
links.added: Personas, inner selves summoned in battle, and a focus on the human psyche.

links.took: Teenagers summoning Personas and negotiating with demons.
links.added: A rumor system where gossip spread around town becomes real.

links.took: Persona summoning and a modern Japanese city setting.
links.added: A school-year calendar, Social Links and the tower dungeon Tartarus.

links.took: Demon negotiation, fusion and a post-apocalyptic Tokyo.
links.added: Cel-shaded 3D, the Press Turn system and a half-demon hero.

links.took: Atlus's weakness-based battles; Persona 3 began after Nocturne was finished.
links.added: Daily school life and friendships that make your Personas stronger.

links.took: The school calendar, Social Links and Persona fusion.
links.added: A small-town murder mystery and dungeons inside a TV world.

links.took: HD development experience; Katsura Hashino called Catherine a test for the next Persona.
links.added: Stylish heists in hand-built Palaces and a Phantom Thieves story.

links.took: Director Katsura Hashino, artist Shigenori Soejima, composer Shoji Meguro and many Persona systems.
links.added: A fantasy kingdom's royal election, Archetype classes and Press Turn battles.
links.extra: Journalists also noted Persona 5's influence on it.

links.took: The Press Turn system, where exploiting weaknesses earns extra turns.
links.added: Press Turn combined with a real-time field attack before battles start.

updates.why: first released in Japan on 15 September 2016

updates.value: Yuji Horii modeled it on Wizardry and Ultima, with Akira Toriyama's art and Koichi Sugiyama's music.
Akitoshi Kawazu based its battles on Dungeons & Dragons and Wizardry; Nasir Gebelli programmed it.
Satoshi Tajiri drew on his childhood hobby of insect collecting; the Game Boy link cable inspired trading.
